title: What High-Potential Team Members Need Most From Leaders
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that leaders instinctively overload their most capable people with additional tasks and responsibilities, which actually stalls their growth rather than accelerating it. It distinguishes potential from capacity, noting high performers aren't limited by effort but by their ability to integrate and reflect on what they're learning. The recommended fix is deliberately creating unstructured space and time rather than piling on more challenges. The piece closes by contrasting execution, which relies on repeatable patterns, with growth, which requires reconfiguring those patterns during quiet, unscheduled time.
points: Leaders often overload high-potential team members with more tasks, which can stall rather than accelerate their growth.
Potential and capacity are different — high performers are constrained by integration and reflection time, not effort.
The most valuable resource for developing top talent is unstructured space and time, not more assignments.
Growth and insight happen between tasks, not during them.
quotes: Surprisingly, what these high-potential team members need most to prosper is often ignored by leaders.
Because high-potential team members are typically more capable than their peers, leaders often load them up with responsibilities, assignments, and new challenges.
The most powerful condition leaders can create for those with the highest potential is more space and time to explore and experiment, not less.
Those with yet unrealized talents need the space to think through and reflect on what they are experiencing.
Insight and growth for high-potential team members happen between tasks, not during them.
When schedules are saturated with tasks, team members can still perform, but they stop evolving.
